title: Premature Speech EOS is Not a Dominant Failure Mode in Qwen2.5-Omni: An Empirical Study of Text-Length-Coupled Audio Stopping

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to test whether coupling speech stopping to generated text length improves speech-text consistency in an end-to-end omni-modal LLM. No prior paper explicitly addresses this purpose. Papers [1], [2], and [16] discuss speech-text alignment or length control, but their objectives differ: [1] focuses on decoding paradigms for joint speech-text modeling, [2] addresses length control for speech translation to match source audio duration, and [16] investigates monotonic alignment constraints in decoder-only TTS models. None of these papers aim to improve speech-text consistency by coupling speech stopping to text length.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, TLC-AS, is a training-free decode-time intervention that computes a minimum audio token floor from text word count and a calibrated words-per-second rate, masking the speech EOS token until the floor is reached. Paper [2] discusses controlling output length in speech translation using word/character counts, which is conceptually similar to the primitive of coupling text length to speech duration. Paper [19] also explores methods for controlling output length in neural encoder-decoder models, which aligns with the underlying mechanism of length-based constraints. Both papers cover the mechanism at the primitive level.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses VoiceBench CommonEval (200 samples) to compare WER with and without the intervention. Papers [1], [2], and [16] employ evaluation setups that involve word error rate (WER) as a metric for speech-text alignment or generation quality. For example, [1] systematically compares decoding strategies using WER, [2] evaluates length-controlled speech translation using WER, and [16] assesses alignment constraints in TTS models using WER. These prior papers reuse the same evaluation design (WER-based comparison), even though the specific benchmark (VoiceBench CommonEval) differs. Thus, the evaluation facet is covered.

### Domain
The domain is omni-modal LLM speech generation. Papers [1], [3], [4], [7], [10], [15], [16], and [20] all operate within the general area of speech generation or text-to-speech synthesis, which includes omni-modal or multi-modal models. While the specific focus or dataset may differ, the application area of speech generation is well-covered by these prior works.
